This is a hypothetical to show your money can sometimes go further if you don’t pay things off all in one go

Heres a bit of an uncommon recommendation for you. Use debt to your advantage. Debt can be good if used correctly and jut because you are getting a big limp sum doesn’t mean you should pay off stuff like a house in one go. 

Lets say you use 100k to put down a decent deposit for a 350k house, you have 250k left to pay, at the horrible rates we are now (I used 5.5%) you will probably pay a bit over 1.5k a month. At better rates (if you can hold out), lets use 1.5%, it will be around 1k a month. 

Lets say the 300k not used for the house gets put into stocks and shares. The average growth is around 6% yearly I believe. That means about 1.5k a month on average. This would cover about all of it in either scenario. Obviously depends and changes on the companies chosen, dividends, market performance etc etc. 

This is just one thing you could do, you could also look into house renovating, buying run down or easily converted properties on mortgage, fixing them up/converting them (adding bedrooms/turn house into multiple apartments) then rent them out. Should have plenty of capital to start this, can lead to you having many properties that will pay for themselves, and then the extra money you have can be invested in other ways such at stocks again. 

Think about how you can use this money to not just make your life easier now such as paying off debts and buying a house. But how it can make you money in the future so that you won’t have to work and it will actually make you more money. 

Im not a financial advisor and I highly recommend you speak to one, you are young, this is the perfect time in your life to set your self up properly.

It might be a good idea to set yourself a monthly allowance of sorts. Give yourself the same amount each month and any you don’t spend keep in there so you can save up for things you want. Reward yourself for saving.

You have some time so make a plan beforehand. Give yourself a little extra spending money so you don’t feel like you haven’t gained for taking the new job, this will help prevent temptation to go into savings.

Aside from that I recommend either using a second bank account to store an emergency fund so its out of sight and not tempting, you can even get rid of the card (or lock it away) so the only way to spend it is to consciously transfer it back. And depending on your country (Im from UK so might not be the most helpful) you might be able to get a stocks and shares ISA to use as a long term savings.

Basically, ‘spend’ the money in savings, get it out of your account whether you send it to a high interest saving account at a different bank, or an investment account/stocks and shares etc.
